title: Parts XI and XVII (concurrency; toolchain, manifest, builds, diagnostics)

found.group: G5: Parts XI and XVII (concurrency; toolchain, manifest, builds, diagnostics)

findings.title: "under a lock" in [THR-11] admits a shared (read) lock and an unnamed kind of place: two tasks change one `shares mut` object under `RwLock.read()`, and two tasks may both consume one `Receiver`
findings.program:
import std.thread
from std.sync import RwLock

class Player:
    hp: int = 10

fn main():
    p = shares mut Player()
    rw = RwLock(shares mut p)
    with scope = thread.scope():
        for _ in 0..2:
            scope.spawn(owns fn():
                with g = rw.read():
                    g.hp = g.hp + 1)        # <-- two tasks write one `hp` at once: `g` is `ref shares mut Player`, which an owner changes through a plain name ([BRW-15]); the change is "under a lock", so [THR-11] accepts it
    with g = rw.read():
        println(g.hp)

# second scenario: two tasks, or a task and the parent, call `rx.recv()` on one `Receiver` (a one-consumer queue): [THR-3] makes `recv()` a change of `rx`, [THR-11]'s list of exceptions does not name a channel end (so two senders on one `tx` would be E7007, which [THR-15]'s "many-producer" forbids), and [THR-13] bullet 3 lists "channel end" among the places that are ordered by themselves.
findings.why: [THR-11]: "two of them changing one place, or one reading a place another changes, is `E7007`, other than by a reduction (`[THR-21]`), under a lock, or through an `Atomic`" — no word says which lock, and an `RwLock`'s `read()` is a lock. [THR-9] says `RwLock[T]` is `ThreadShared` only "for a `T` that is `Send` and `ThreadShared`", but no rule of §XI.3 requires the places a scoped task reaches to be `ThreadShared`; a task "uses the caller's real variables". [THR-13] bullet 3: "an `Atomic`, `Mutex`, `RwLock`, channel end or `guarded by` field: ordered by the atomic or by the lock" — a `Receiver` is a channel end, yet [THR-15] says it is a one-consumer queue and `Receiver` is `Send` but not `ThreadShared`. [THR-3]: "A `Mutex`, `RwLock`, `Atomic` or channel end is changed through any name, a plain one included, by its own operations".
findings.proposed_text: In `[THR-11]`, replace "is `E7007`, other than by a reduction (`[THR-21]`), under a lock, or through an `Atomic`." with: "is `E7007`, other than by a reduction (`[THR-21]`) or through a value of a `ThreadShared` type by its own operations (`[THR-9]`): an `Atomic`; a `Lock` and the fields `guarded by` it; a `Mutex[T]` for a `Send` `T`; an `RwLock[T]` for a `T` that is `Send` and `ThreadShared` (its `read()` guard is a `ref T` several tasks hold at once, so a `T` one thread changes through any owner, `shares mut Player`, is not enough); a `Sender`. A `Receiver` is not `ThreadShared`: it is used by one task, or by the parent, until the join, as any other place (`E7007`: \"two tasks take values out of `rx`, which one consumer owns; give each task a channel of its own, or let one task receive and hand the values on\"). A read lock on a value one thread changes through any owner is refused with the lock that fits: \"`rw` holds a `shares mut Player`, which any owner changes, so two tasks holding `rw.read()` could change `p.hp` at once; keep the player inside the lock: write `rw = RwLock(Player())` in place of line 9 and `with g = rw.write():` in place of line 13\"." In `[THR-13]` bullet 3, replace "an `Atomic`, `Mutex`, `RwLock`, channel end or `guarded by` field" with "an `Atomic`, a `Mutex`, an `RwLock` whose content is `ThreadShared`, a `Sender` or a `guarded by` field". In `[THR-20]`, replace "(`Lock`, `Atomic`, `Mutex`, `RwLock`, a channel end)" with "(`Lock`, `Atomic`, `Mutex`, `RwLock`, a `Sender`; a `Receiver` is not `ThreadShared`, `E7002`)".
findings.codes: E7007 reused (two tasks change one place); E7002 reused for a `static Receiver`

findings.title: A scoped task may end a `shares` owner, or end an object a `weakref` link names, with plain count writes while the parent touches the same header
findings.program:
import std.thread

class Player:
    name: String = String("ann")

fn main():
    p = shares Player()
    a: Array[shares Player] = [shares p]
    b: Array[shares Player] = [shares p]
    with scope = thread.scope():
        scope.spawn(owns fn(): a.clear())    # <-- ends a's owner of the player: a plain subtract in the player's header, on the task's thread
        b.clear()                             # <-- ends b's owner on the main thread at the same time: two plain read-modify-writes of one count race (a lost subtract leaks the player; `[OWN-2]`)

fn main2():
    q = Player()
    w = weakref q
    with scope = thread.scope():
        scope.spawn(owns fn(): q = Player())  # <-- replaces the parent's `q`: the old player is ended on the task's thread (its ended mark written, its weak count read, plain)
        if w exists as r:                      # <-- tests the same header on the main thread at the same time; the test may pass and `r.name` is read while the task frees the old player's fields
            println(r.name)

# [THR-11] accepts both: in the first, the task changes `a` and the parent `b`, two places; in the second, the task changes `q` and the parent reads `w`. Neither line makes a `shares` owner or makes, ends or opens a `weakref` link in the task, which is all [THR-11] forbids.
findings.why: [THR-11]: "A task makes, ends or opens a `weakref` link only to a `thread_shared` target, and makes no `shares` owner (`[THR-2]`)" — ending a `shares` owner, and ending an object that links name, are not named. [THR-2]: "A `shares` or `shares mut` owner counts its owners with plain adds, and every object that is not `thread_shared` counts its `weakref` links with plain adds." [WK-11]: "That count is a number in the target's header that no name reads, so making or ending a link is not a change of the target" — so the header is not a place [THR-11]'s check sees. [RC-5] point 1 forbids an end only "in the view's life", a sequential notion, and the parent's `if w exists as r:` runs beside the task, not after it. Whether `scope.spawn(owns fn() owns q: ...)` is "an object handed whole to another thread" (the compare and move of [THR-2]) is also unsaid: [THR-2] names only `thread.spawn`, and without the move a hand-over to a task gives the same race.
findings.proposed_text: Add to `[THR-11]`, after "and makes no `shares` owner (`[THR-2]`).": "**A one-thread value's header is a place the tasks of a scope share.** Ending an owner of a `shares` or `shares mut` value, and ending an object (its last owner ending, replaced, or cleared with the list that owns it, and a hand-over of it to another thread, `[THR-2]`), write its header with plain instructions, and making, ending or opening a `weakref` link to it, or making or ending another `shares` owner of it, read or write the same header. So a task that may end a `shares` or `shares mut` owner of a `T`, or end a `T` object, while the parent or another task may, before that task's join, make or end a `shares` owner of a `T`, make, end or open a `weakref T` link, or end a `T` object, is `E7007`, by class family (the compiler cannot tell which object a link or an owner names): \"the task started on line 11 may end a `Player` (`a.clear()`), and line 12 ends one too (`b.clear()`), each with a plain write to the player's count; end one after the join: move line 12 below the `with scope` block\"; \"the task started on line 18 may end the `Player` `w` links (`q = Player()`), while line 19 tests whether it still lives; open `w` after the `with scope` block, or join the task first: write `h = scope.spawn(...)` on line 18 and `h.join()` above line 19\". A `thread_shared` target is not such a place: its counts are atomic and an opened view holds one (`[RC-5]` point 2). A value handed to a task or a job with `owns` is handed to another thread: `[THR-2]`'s compare and move apply at the spawn, so every link on this thread then finds it ended, and the task's end of it touches no header this thread reads." In `[THR-2]`, replace "**An object handed whole to another thread leaves its `weakref` links behind**" with "**An object handed whole to another thread, a scoped task or a job included, leaves its `weakref` links behind**".
findings.codes: E7007 reused (the header as a place two tasks share)

findings.title: A one-thread `weakref` link to an object a `thread_shared` value owns: the object ends on whichever thread's owner is last, racing the link's test (extends O2, O1)
findings.program:
import std.thread
from std.sync import Lock

class Player:
    name: String = String("ann")

class Team:
    lock: Lock = Lock()
    players: Array[Player] guarded by lock = []

fn main():
    team = thread_shared Team(players=[Player()])
    with team.lock:
        w = weakref team.players[0]        # <-- a one-thread link (plain weak count, plain test) to a player the shared team owns
    h = thread.spawn(owns fn() thread_shared team: pass)
    team = thread_shared Team()            # main's owner ends; the player now ends on whichever thread ends the team's last owner ([THR-20]: "A drop runs where the last owner ends")
    if w exists as p:                      # <-- the test of the player's header runs on main while the other thread may be ending the player: the test can pass, and `p.name` is read while its String is freed
        println(p.name)
    h.join()
findings.why: [THR-1] bullet 2 checks only what the value holds: "everything reachable from it is `Send` (`[THR-8]`): a one-thread owner, a `weakref` link to a value that is not `thread_shared`, or a plain `fn()` value reachable from it is `E7015`" — a `Player` with one owner is `Send`, and the link is held outside the team, not reachable from it. [THR-2] forbids a link only "in a scoped task, a job, or any function that may run on another thread than its target's owner"; `main` runs on a thread that owns the team, so the line is allowed. [THR-20]: "The last owner of a `thread_shared` value may end on any thread that holds a count of it ... counts as possibly running that value's `drop`, and the `drop` of everything it owns" — which is the player's end on another thread. [WK-11]: "Its target lives on its own: a class object" — a player owned by a team qualifies. O2 proposes `weakref thread_shared T` for a `thread_shared` target, and O1(c) names "reachable from a `thread_shared` value" for the walk region only; neither says that a one-thread link may not name an object a `thread_shared` value owns.
findings.proposed_text: Add to `[THR-1]` bullet 2, after "is `E7015` at the line that makes it `thread_shared`": "; and no `weakref` link that is not to a `thread_shared` target names an object the value owns, directly or through what it owns, all the way down: such an object ends on the thread that ends the value's last owner (`[THR-20]`), while a one-thread link tests its header with plain instructions. A link made through a `thread_shared` name or parameter (`weakref team.players[0]`) is `E7015` at the link (\"`team` is shared between threads (line 12), so the player it owns may end on any of them, and `w` would test whether it lives with no atomic; share the player too: write `players: Array[thread_shared Player] guarded by lock = []` in `Team`, `Team(players=[thread_shared Player()])` on line 12, and `w = weakref team.players[0]` then links a `thread_shared` target\"); and a value is made `thread_shared` only when no class it may own, by the types of its fields all the way down, is one a `weakref` link in the program names with a one-thread link (the same class families as `[THR-2]`'s hand-over compare; across a package's edge, the class is `pub` or the package's own link names it, O1), `E7015` at the line that makes it `thread_shared`, with the same words." Add to `[WK-11]`: "Its target ends on the thread that holds the link: a class object or `shares` value no `thread_shared` value owns, or a `thread_shared` value itself (`[THR-1]`)."
findings.codes: E7015 reused (a one-thread link reaching another thread); needs O2's `weakref thread_shared T` for the fix line

findings.title: A dependency's manifest chooses the C compiler flags, link inputs and C++ project configuration the builder's toolchain runs with: build-time code execution that [CT-2]'s sandbox (F15) does not cover
findings.program:
# the dependency `parser`'s ember.toml, fetched by `[dependencies] parser = { git = "https://example.org/parser.git", rev = "4f2a9c1" }`
[package]
name = "parser"
version = "0.1.0"

[c]
compiler = "clang"
flags = ["-fplugin=./vendor/helper.so"]    # <-- the builder's C compiler loads and runs the dependency's code while compiling the shim of `unsafe import c "./shim.c"`; `-specs=`, `-Xclang -load`, `-include /home/.../secret.h` do the same

[link]
libs = ["./vendor/libhelper.a"]            # link inputs the root never named

[cpp.parser]
# a C++ project configured and read "through the CMake File API" (Annex C): configuring runs the project's CMake code on the builder's machine
findings.why: [MAN-8]: "The sections are: ... `[c]` (`compiler`, `flags`, `[BLD-FFI-1]`); `[link]` (`libs`, `timeout` `[BLD-15]`); ... `[cpp.<project>]` and `[ffi]`" — for every package's manifest, with no word on whether a dependency's sections are honoured. [BLD-FFI-1]: "The manifest's `[c]` section names the C compiler and flags used for shims and C source files"; [BLD-FFI-1a]: "Each `import c` is parsed and its shim compiled with the package's C flags plus the import's own `defines` and `include_paths`" — "the package's", so the dependency's own flags run the builder's compiler. [CT-2] (F15) sandboxes a dependency's compile-time Ember code "so a dependency's build cannot read the builder's files" and "cannot read the builder's environment"; the same dependency reaches both through a compiler flag. [MAN-8]'s last sentence, "No manifest key turns off a safety check or changes what a program means", does not reach what runs while building.
findings.proposed_text: Add `[MAN-10]` after `[MAN-8]`: "**A dependency's manifest decides only its own code, never what runs on the builder's machine.** Of a dependency's manifest the build reads `[package]`, `[dependencies]`, `[lints]`, `[realtime]` and `[ffi]`. Its `[c]` section is taken with `compiler` ignored (the root's, or the backend's, `[BLD-FFI-1]`) and `flags` limited to `-D<name>[=<value>]`, `-U<name>`, `-I<path>` for a path under the dependency's own root, `-std=<c-standard>`, `-W…` and `-O<n>`; its `[link] libs` are taken for names (`\"m\"`) and for paths under its own root; and its `[cpp.<project>]` section, any other `[c] flags` entry, any other `[link]` path, and its `[build]`, `[profiles]`, `[jobs]`, `[comptime]` sections are honoured only when the root package's manifest names the dependency in `[build] native = [\"parser\"]`, and are `E9001` otherwise, naming the dependency, the key and the line to add: \"`parser`'s manifest sets `[c] flags = [\\\"-fplugin=./vendor/helper.so\\\"]`, which would run its code inside this build's C compiler; a dependency's flags are limited to defines, include paths under its root, a C standard and warnings; to take the rest as written, add `native = [\\\"parser\\\"]` under `[build]` in `ember.toml`\". `ember tcb` lists every dependency so named (`[TCB-4]`, external library)." In `[BLD-FFI-1a]`, replace "with the package's C flags" with "with the package's C flags as `[MAN-10]` admits them".
findings.codes: E9001 reused (invalid manifest, naming the key and what is accepted); a new `[build] native` key in [MAN-8]'s list

findings.title: A thread's, task's or job's function that gives a capture away is a `once fn`, and `spawn`/`submit` are typed `thread_shared fn() -> R` / `fn() -> R`
findings.program:
import std.thread
from std.sync import Receiver, channel

fn drain(owns rx: Receiver[int]) -> int:
    total = 0
    for v in owns rx:
        total += v
    return total

fn main():
    tx, rx = channel[int](capacity=4)
    h = thread.spawn(owns fn() owns rx: drain(owns rx))   # <-- this function gives `rx` away, so its type is `once fn() -> int` ([CLO-6]); `spawn` takes `owns f: thread_shared fn() -> R`, which is not a `once fn` parameter: does the call compile?
    tx.send(owns 3).unwrap()
    println(h.join())
findings.why: [THR-10]: "`[R]` above `pub fn spawn(owns f: thread_shared fn() -> R) -> JoinHandle[R]:`"; [THR-11]: "`fn spawn(owns f: fn() -> R) -> ScopedJoinHandle[R]:`"; [JOB-2]: "`pub fn submit(owns f: thread_shared fn()) -> JobHandle:`". [CLO-6]: "A function that gives one of its captures away (to an `owns` parameter, a return, a field) can be called only once. Its type is `once fn(A) -> R`, not `fn(A) -> R`; given where a function may run twice it is `E3013` ... A parameter that takes a `once fn` holds it, `owns f: once fn(A) -> R`, and accepts both kinds". [FN-6]: "Callable types are compared by their parameter types and words, their result, `unsafe` and `thread_shared`" — `once` is not named among what is compared, and whether a `once fn` coerces to `fn()` is unsaid. A compiler must choose between refusing the most common thread body (one that consumes what it was handed) and accepting a `once` value where the type says `fn()`.
findings.proposed_text: In `[THR-10]`, replace "`[R]` above `pub fn spawn(owns f: thread_shared fn() -> R) -> JoinHandle[R]:`" with "`[R]` above `pub fn spawn(owns f: thread_shared once fn() -> R) -> JoinHandle[R]:`, which runs it once and so accepts a function that gives its captures away as well as one that does not (`[CLO-6]`)". In `[THR-11]`: "`fn spawn(owns f: once fn() -> R) -> ScopedJoinHandle[R]:`". In `[JOB-2]`: "`s.submit` on a `JobScope` takes a plain function (`owns f: once fn()`)" and "`pub fn submit(owns f: thread_shared once fn()) -> JobHandle:`"; `[JOB-3]`'s `submit_after` the same. In `[CLO-7]`, replace "`thread.spawn` and `jobs.submit` take `owns f: thread_shared fn() -> R`" with "`thread.spawn` and `jobs.submit` take `owns f: thread_shared once fn() -> R`" and "`scope.spawn` a plain `owns f: fn() -> R`" with "`scope.spawn` a plain `owns f: once fn() -> R`". In `[FN-6]`, add `once` to "compared by their parameter types and words, their result, `unsafe`, `once` and `thread_shared`", and: "a `fn(…)` coerces to the `once fn(…)` of the same shape; a `once fn(…)` never to `fn(…)` (`E3013`)".
findings.codes: E3013 reused; the signatures of `spawn`, `submit`, `submit_after` change (text and `std`)

findings.title: The written form of a `max`/`min`/`add` reduction, the accumulator of `m[k] op= e`, and whether a `static mut` or a `thread_shared` field is a reduction place are unsaid
findings.program:
import std.thread

static mut SEEN: int = 0

fn main():
    best = 0
    counts: Map[String, int] = {}
    parts = [String("ab"), String("c")]
    with scope = thread.scope():
        for part in parts:
            scope.spawn(owns fn() ref part:
                best = max(best, part.len())     # <-- is this the `max` reduction of [THR-21], or "a task that reads the current value" (E7007)? No form for `max` is written
                counts[part] += 1                 # <-- `m[k] op= e`: `k` differs per task; "each task's accumulator has the place's type" names an `int`, so what is combined at the join, and what if `part` is not a key yet?
                SEEN += 1)                        # <-- [THR-20] says a `static mut` the tasks reach may change "by a reduction"; [THR-21] names "a local, or a field of an object the tasks reach"
    println(best, counts, SEEN)
findings.why: [THR-21]: "A task's `total += e` (and `-=`, `*=`, `|=`, `&=`, `^=`, `max`, `min`, `push`, `extend`, `add`, `m[k] op= e`) on a local, or on a field of an object the tasks reach ... is a reduction" and "Each task's accumulator has the place's type"; also "a task that reads the current value (`if stats.total < 10: stats.total += x`) need[s] a lock (`E7007`)" — `best = max(best, e)` reads the current value. [THR-20]: "two tasks changing it, or one reading what another changes, is `E7007`, other than by a reduction, under a lock or through an `Atomic`" — a `static mut` is neither a local nor a field. [THR-1]: "no owner changes a `thread_shared` value directly (`E7014`)" — [THR-21] does not say that `st.total += x` on a `thread_shared st` is a direct change, so the combining write at the join is either `E7014` or admitted.
findings.proposed_text: Replace in `[THR-21]` "A task's `total += e` (and `-=`, `*=`, `|=`, `&=`, `^=`, `max`, `min`, `push`, `extend`, `add`, `m[k] op= e`) on a local, or on a field of an object the tasks reach (`scope.spawn(owns fn() copy of x: stats.total += x)`), a field reached through two `sharedref mut` links to one object included, is a reduction" with: "A task's statement of one of these forms on a place `P` that the task otherwise neither reads nor writes — `P op= e` for `+`, `-`, `*`, `|`, `&`, `^`; `P = max(P, e)` and `P = min(P, e)`; `P.push(owns e)`, `P.extend(owns e)` and `P.add(owns e)`; and `P[k] op= e` on a `Map` — where `P` is a local, a `static mut` (`[THR-20]`), or a field of an object the tasks reach (`scope.spawn(owns fn() copy of x: stats.total += x)`), a field reached through two `sharedref mut` links to one object included, is a reduction. A field of a `thread_shared` value is not: the combining write at the join is a direct change (`E7014`, `[THR-1]`), and the message gives the `Atomic` or the `guarded by` field. For `P[k] op= e` the accumulator is a `Map` of the task's own keys, and the join applies `P[k] op= acc[k]` for each key in spawn order, inserting a key absent from `P` with the accumulator's value." Keep the rest of the rule as it is.
findings.touches_owner_verdict: 105 is kept (the accumulator's type and its overflow stop are unchanged)

findings.title: [THR-19] refuses waits only "inside a lock's `with` block": a guard held in a plain local, a foreign call that may run a kept callback, a static's first-access initialiser and `read()` under `read()` are unsaid
findings.program:
from std.sync import Mutex

static mut HANDLER: fn() = fn(): pass

fn main():
    m = Mutex(0)
    g = m.lock()                 # <-- the lock is held by a local, not a `with` block, until `g`'s last use
    HANDLER()                    # <-- may run a stored function that takes `m`'s lock ([THR-19] names such a call only "inside a lock's `with` block"): waits for ever, and nothing refuses it
    println(g)

# the same question for: a foreign call not marked `@ffi(no_callbacks)` inside `with log.lock:` (it may run a callback C keeps that takes `log`'s lock, [EFF-26]); a first access of `static REG: Mutex[Map[String, int]] = build()` whose `build` takes a lock this thread holds ([STA-3] runs it on first access, which is not a call); and `rw.read()` while this thread holds `rw.read()` with a writer waiting between them.
findings.why: [THR-19]: "Inside a lock's `with` block, these are `E7018`, with no loop needed and nothing checked while the program runs: a call through a function value, or through a `dyn` or `virtual` method, that may run a function taking a lock of the kind this thread holds ... a join ... and a direct call that may take the held lock" — the condition is the `with` block, and the list has no foreign call and no first access. [THR-3]: "`m.lock()` blocks and returns a `MutexGuard[T]`, a view of `m` ... the mutex is released when the guard ends, which `with g = m.lock():` places at the end of the block" — a guard in a plain local is legal and ends at its block's end. [THR-19] (F21) names "its `write()` while this thread holds its `read()`, or the reverse" and not a second `read()`, whose outcome depends on whether the runtime's `RwLock` lets a waiting writer block new readers. [STA-3]: "Any other initialiser runs once, on first access ... the first access blocks until it completes."
findings.proposed_text: In `[THR-19]`, replace "Inside a lock's `with` block, these are `E7018`" with "While this thread holds a lock — inside its `with` block, or from `g = m.lock()`, `g = rw.read()` or `g = rw.write()` to the last use of `g` or of a value holding it (`[BRW-2]`) — these are `E7018`". Extend the list: "a foreign call not declared `@ffi(no_callbacks)`, which may run a callback C keeps that takes such a lock (`[EFF-26]`); a first access of a `static` whose initialiser runs on first access (`[STA-3]`), which counts as a direct call of that initialiser; a second `read()` of an `RwLock` this thread holds `read()`, since a writer that arrived between the two would wait for the first and the second for it (\"`rw.read()` (line 9) takes a read lock this thread already holds (line 7), and a writer arriving between them would make each wait for the other for ever; use the guard `g` already held, or take the second read after the first ends\")".

findings.title: `with x.lock:` holds no view of `x.lock`: the lock may be replaced, swapped or taken out, and `x` ended, while the block holds it
findings.program:
from std.sync import Lock

class Log:
    lock: Lock = Lock()
    lines: Array[String] guarded by lock = []

fn main():
    log = Log()
    with log.lock:
        log.lock = Lock()                    # <-- replaces the lock this block holds: the block's end unlocks a lock never taken, and the one that was taken is gone; no rule names a view of `log.lock` that `[BRW-1]` would protect
        log.lines.push(owns String("a"))
    with log.lock:                           # a lock in an undefined state
        println(log.lines.len())
findings.why: [THR-18]: "A `Lock` is a lock with no value inside; `with x.lock:` holds it for the block." — nothing says the block holds a view of `x.lock`, and a `Lock` field is not a `let` field, so `log.lock = Lock()` is an ordinary change of a field through an owner. [THR-3] gives `with g = m.lock():` a guard that is "a view of `m` that reads through to `ref mut T` (`[TYP-14]`)", which `[BRW-1]` protects; the `Lock` form has no name and so no view. Whether a `Lock`, `Mutex`, `RwLock`, `Atomic` or `Once` may be given another value at all is unsaid.
findings.proposed_text: Add to `[THR-18]`, after "`with x.lock:` holds it for the block.": "The block holds a read-only view of `x.lock` whose life is the block, as `with g = m.lock():` holds `g` (`[TYP-14]`, `[BRW-1]`): while it runs, `x.lock` is not given another value, swapped or taken out, and `x` is not handed over, ended or given another value, through any name (`E3021`: \"`log.lock = Lock()` (line 10) replaces the lock this block holds (line 9); the block's end would release a lock never taken; give the log a new lock after the block, or never: a lock is made with its object\"). A `Lock`, `Mutex`, `RwLock`, `Atomic` or `Once` field is set in `init` and never replaced after it, as a `let` field is (`E3023`, shape N7); a local of one of these types is given another value only when no guard of it is in use."
findings.codes: E3021 reused (a change of what a read-only view reads); E3023 reused for the field

findings.title: [BLD-14]'s recorded facts name "the locks a function may take" but not the locks it needs held ([THR-18], [EFF-24])
findings.program:
# library L
pub class Log:
    lock: Lock = Lock()
    lines: Array[String] guarded by lock = []

pub fn count(log: Log) -> int:
    return log.lines.len()          # uses a guarded field without the lock: `count` needs `log.lock` held ([THR-18])

# program D, another package
n = count(log)                        # <-- without `with log.lock:`; whether D's compiler knows `count` needs the lock depends on which of [BLD-14] item 6 and [EFF-24] it reads
findings.why: [BLD-14] item 6: "the locks a function may take;" [EFF-24]: "and which locks it may take, or needs held (`[THR-18]`)"; [THR-18]: "A function whose body uses a guarded field without taking its lock is worked out to need that lock held (its summary, `[EFF-24]`), and is called only where the lock is held (`E7013`)". `[EFF-4]` records "the summary" whole, so the fact is recorded by one rule and left out by the other's list.
findings.proposed_text: In `[BLD-14]`, replace "6. the locks a function may take; and" with "6. the locks a function may take, and the locks it needs held (`[THR-18]`); and".

findings.title: [PRF-1] says only `debug_assert` differs between profiles, and [PRF-3] allows C sanitizers in `debug` and `development`, which stop the program where `release` does not
findings.program:
# ember.toml
[profiles.development]
sanitizers = ["address"]
# a foreign call that writes one byte past a buffer C owns stops the `development` build with the sanitizer's report and runs on in `release`: [PRF-1] promises every profile "stops in the same places with the same messages"
findings.why: [PRF-1]: "Every profile accepts the same programs, performs the same safety checks while the program runs (`[PRF-4]`), stops in the same places with the same messages, and computes the same results. The one check that differs is `debug_assert`". [PRF-3]'s table: "C sanitizers (`sanitizers = […]`) | allowed | allowed | not allowed". [PRF-4]: "The checks that run while a program runs are the same in every profile".
findings.proposed_text: In `[PRF-1]`, after "The one check that differs is `debug_assert`, checked only where `[PRF-3]` says", add: "; a C sanitizer (`[PRF-3]`) is a tool for finding defects in foreign and `unsafe` code, outside Ember's checks: it stops the program only where that code is already outside the guarantee (`[PHIL-10]`), and never changes where Safe Ember stops."

findings.title: `ember run --interp` says threads are unavailable and nothing about `@parallel` loops and `std.jobs`

[PAR-5]: "A `@parallel` loop therefore computes the same bits whatever the worker count and scheduling". [CT-2]'s `E6010` names "a thread". verdicts.reason: Scenario 1 (two tasks write `hp` through `rw.read()`) is refused by the text: `[THR-3]` makes `read()` "a shared guard, `ref T`", so `g` is a plain local holding a view, and `[BRW-15]` says "a plain local that holds a view never change[s] what they name or what it leads to (a `Cell` field, an object behind a `shares` link, the elements of a `MutSpan`). A change through one is `E3023`"; `[CELL-1]` repeats it for a `Cell` ("through a plain name, `E3023`, `[BRW-15]`"). So `g.hp = g.hp + 1` is `E3023` whatever the lock, and no `ThreadShared` requirement on a scoped task's reach is needed. Scenario 2 is real: `[THR-3]` ("A `Mutex`, `RwLock`, `Atomic` or channel end is changed through any name ... by its own operations") makes `rx.recv()` and `tx.send()` changes of `rx`/`tx`; `[THR-11]`'s exceptions are only "by a reduction (`[THR-21]`), under a lock, or through an `Atomic`", so two tasks on one `tx` read literally as `E7007` against `[THR-15]`'s many-producer `ThreadShared` `Sender`, while `[THR-13]` bullet 3 ("an `Atomic`, `Mutex`, `RwLock`, channel end or `guarded by` field: ordered by the atomic or by the lock") and `[THR-20]` ("`Lock`, `Atomic`, `Mutex`, `RwLock`, a channel end") read a channel end as self-ordered, which would admit two tasks calling `recv()` on a one-consumer `Receiver` that `[THR-15]` says is `Send` but not `ThreadShared`, a marker no scoped-task rule consults. A compiler must guess both ways. The `[THR-20]` edit is editorial only: a `static Receiver` is already `E7002` by `[STA-1]` ("`T` MUST be `ThreadShared` (`E7002`)").
verdicts.narrowed_to: `[THR-11]` does not say whether a channel end's own operations are among its exceptions, so two tasks (or a task and the parent) calling `send` on one `Sender` read as `E7007` while two calling `recv` on one `Receiver` read as admitted by `[THR-13]` bullet 3; `[THR-13]`'s and `[THR-20]`'s "channel end" must become `Sender`.
verdicts.better_fix: In `[THR-11]`, replace "is `E7007`, other than by a reduction (`[THR-21]`), under a lock, or through an `Atomic`." with "is `E7007`, other than by a reduction (`[THR-21]`), through the lock that guards the place (a `guarded by` field inside `with` its lock, `[THR-18]`; a `Mutex`'s or `RwLock`'s content through its guard, `[THR-3]`), through an `Atomic`, or through a `Sender` by its own operations (`[THR-15]`). A `Receiver` is one consumer: it is used by one task, or by the parent, until the join, as any other place (`E7007`: \"two tasks take values out of `rx`, which one consumer owns; give each task a channel of its own, or let one task receive and hand the values on\")." In `[THR-13]` bullet 3, replace "an `Atomic`, `Mutex`, `RwLock`, channel end or `guarded by` field" with "an `Atomic`, `Mutex`, `RwLock`, `Sender` or `guarded by` field". In `[THR-20]`, replace "(`Lock`, `Atomic`, `Mutex`, `RwLock`, a channel end)" with "(`Lock`, `Atomic`, `Mutex`, `RwLock`, a `Sender`; a `Receiver` is not `ThreadShared`, `E7002`, `[STA-1]`)". The `E7007` registry row gains "through a `Sender`". No change to `[THR-9]`'s `RwLock` sentence is needed.

verdicts.reason: Nothing refuses either program. `[THR-11]` forbids in a task only that it "makes, ends or opens a `weakref` link only to a `thread_shared` target, and makes no `shares` owner"; ending a `shares` owner (`a.clear()`) and ending an object a link names (`q = Player()`) are not named. `[THR-2]`'s routes ("captured or held by a function any thread may run (`thread_shared fn()`, the function of `thread.spawn` or `jobs.submit`, a callback C may run on another thread), handed to an unscoped thread or a job, or reachable from a `thread_shared` value") do not include a scoped task's use of the caller's real variables, and its hand-over compare names `thread.spawn` only. `[RC-4]`: "The counts of a value that is not `thread_shared` are changed with plain adds and subtracts, and never cross threads (`E7015`)" states the promise but names no check for a task. `[WK-11]` removes the header from the places `[THR-11]` compares: "That count is a number in the target's header that no name reads, so making or ending a link is not a change of the target"; `[THR-13]`'s seven kinds of place do not list a header. `[RC-5]` point 1 refuses an end only by "a line or call in the view's life", and the spawn on line 18 is before `r`'s life. So a task and the parent subtract one plain count at once (a lost subtract leaks or double-frees), and the parent's `if w exists as r:` can pass while the task frees the player.
verdicts.better_fix: A one-sided rule on the task is enough, since the parent and the other tasks then never share a one-thread header with it. Add to `[THR-11]`, replacing "A task makes, ends or opens a `weakref` link only to a `thread_shared` target, and makes no `shares` owner (`[THR-2]`).": "**A task touches no one-thread count.** Making or ending a `shares` or `shares mut` owner, making, ending or opening a `weakref` link, and ending an object a `weakref` link may name (its class family carries a weak count, `[OBJ-1]`), each write a header with plain instructions (`[RC-4]`, `[WK-11]`), which the parent may write at the same moment. So a task does each of them only for a `thread_shared` target (`[THR-2]`), worked out from its body and every function it may run (`[EFF-24]`, `[DRP-8]`): a task that may end a `shares` owner, or may end an object of a class family some `weakref` link names, is `E7015` at the spawn (\"the task started on line 11 clears `a`, which holds `shares Player` owners, whose count is kept with plain adds on one thread; clear it after the join: move `a.clear()` below the `with scope` block\"; \"the task started on line 18 may end the `Player` that `w` links (`q = Player()`), while this thread may test `w`; give `q` its new value after the `with scope` block\"). A value a task or a job takes with `owns` is handed to another thread: `[THR-2]`'s compare and move happen at the spawn, so every link on this thread then finds it ended, and the task ends it with no header this thread reads." In `[THR-2]`, replace "**An object handed whole to another thread leaves its `weakref` links behind**" with "**An object handed whole to another thread, a scoped task or a job included, leaves its `weakref` links behind**". The class-family set is `[THR-2]`'s hand-over set (O1(b) applies to it as it does there).

verdicts.reason: `[THR-1]` bullet 2 checks only what the value holds: "everything reachable from it is `Send` (`[THR-8]`): a one-thread owner, a `weakref` link to a value that is not `thread_shared`, or a plain `fn()` value reachable from it is `E7015`"; the link `w` is held outside the team. `[WK-11]` allows the link ("Its target lives on its own: a class object"; `[THR-2]` itself writes `cam.target = weakref level.enemies[0]`), and `[BRW-20]` confines only views, not links, to `with x.lock:`. `[THR-2]` restricts a link "in a scoped task, a job, or any function that may run on another thread than its target's owner": a sentence about where a function runs, which a compiler judging `main` (the main thread) cannot turn into a fact about an owner that is itself owned by threads it cannot see; and it says nothing for a link made before the value is made `thread_shared` (`p = Player(); w = weakref p; team = thread_shared Team(players=[p])`). `[THR-20]` then states the race: "The last owner of a `thread_shared` value may end on any thread that holds a count of it ... counts as possibly running that value's `drop`, and the `drop` of everything it owns", while `[WK-12]`'s test of a one-thread target is plain. `[WK-18]` already names "not reachable from a `thread_shared` value" as the condition for an object no other thread can end, so the text knows the case and leaves the link unrefused. Neither O1(c) nor O2 covers a one-thread link from outside to an owned object. The reader's second clause (refuse `thread_shared` whenever a one-thread link to an owned class exists anywhere) is O1's whole-program shape and would refuse `thread_shared Team` for a `weakref Player` in an unrelated module; the mechanism the owner already approved (verdict 114, which this extends and does not reverse) does it with one compare per owned object of a linked class.
verdicts.better_fix: Add to `[THR-2]`, after "it is allowed only for a `thread_shared` target, whose counts are kept for several threads and whose opened view holds a count": "; and a link made through a `thread_shared` name or parameter, or through a guard or `guarded by` field of a value reached through one (`weakref team.players[0]`), names an object that may end on any thread that holds the value (`[THR-20]`), so it is `E7015` at the link (\"`team` is shared between threads (line 12), so the player it owns may end on any of them, and `w` would test whether it lives with no atomic; share the player too: write `players: Array[thread_shared Player] guarded by lock = []` in `Team` and `Team(players=[thread_shared Player()])` on line 12\")." And after the hand-over paragraph's "so after `cam.target = weakref level.enemies[0]`, handing `level` over leaves `cam.target` finding enemy 0 ended.": "**Making a value `thread_shared` is such a hand-over for the objects it owns**: at `team = thread_shared Team(players=[p])` the same compare, and move with a link, is made for every object the value owns whose class a `weakref` is made to, so `w = weakref p` made before that line finds the player ended afterwards, and the object the shared team owns has no one-thread link." The fix line needs O2's `weakref thread_shared T` only if the programmer wants to keep a link; the message above needs none.

verdicts.reason: `[MAN-8]` lists `[c]` (`compiler`, `flags`), `[link]` (`libs`) and `[cpp.<project>]` for every manifest and says nothing of whose manifest; `[BLD-FFI-1]` ("The manifest's `[c]` section names the C compiler and flags used for shims and C source files") and `[BLD-FFI-1a]` ("compiled with the package's C flags plus the import's own `defines` and `include_paths`, and no others") bind the flags to the package that owns the `import c`, so a dependency's `-fplugin=`, `-specs=` or `-include` runs on the builder's machine. `[CT-2]` sandboxes only the evaluator ("so a dependency's build cannot read the builder's files", "cannot read the builder's environment"), `[FFI-55]` only the headers a dependency's overlays were checked against, and `[TCB-4]` lists external libraries without any gate. `[MAN-8]`'s "No manifest key turns off a safety check or changes what a program means" does not reach what runs while building. Nothing in Parts XVI, XVII or Annex C limits a dependency's `[c]`, `[link]` or `[cpp.<project>]`. The proposed allowlist is general; two of its admitted flag families must be narrowed, since `-W` admits `-Wl,` (linker arguments: `-Wl,-rpath`, `-Wl,--wrap`), `-Wa,` and `-Wp,`, and `-I<path>` must resolve symbolic links as `[CT-2]` does.
verdicts.better_fix: As proposed, with these changes to `[MAN-10]`: "`flags` limited to `-D<name>[=<value>]`, `-U<name>`, `-I<path>` for a path that, with every symbolic link followed, lies under the dependency's own root (`[CT-2]`), `-std=<c-standard>`, `-O<n>`, and `-W<name>` other than `-Wl,…`, `-Wa,…` and `-Wp,…`, which pass arguments to the linker, assembler and preprocessor"; and `[link] libs` entries "for names with no path separator (`\"m\"`) and for paths under its own root, resolved the same way". Keep the `E9001` message and the `[build] native = ["parser"]` key, added to `[MAN-8]`'s `[build]` list; `ember tcb` lists each so named under external library (`[TCB-4]`).

verdicts.reason: `[CLO-6]`: "A function that gives one of its captures away (to an `owns` parameter, a return, a field) can be called only once. Its type is `once fn(A) -> R`, not `fn(A) -> R`; given where a function may run twice it is `E3013` ... A parameter that takes a `once fn` holds it, `owns f: once fn(A) -> R`, and accepts both kinds". `[THR-10]` writes `pub fn spawn(owns f: thread_shared fn() -> R)`, `[THR-11]` `fn spawn(owns f: fn() -> R)`, `[JOB-2]` `pub fn submit(owns f: thread_shared fn())` and "`owns f: fn()`", and `[CLO-7]` repeats them: none is a `once fn` parameter, so `thread.spawn(owns fn() owns rx: drain(owns rx))` is by the letter `E3013` (or `E2020`), refusing the thread body that consumes what it was handed, while `[ERR-4]` (Part XIII) shows the intended pattern for such parameters (`[F: needs once fn(owns T) -> U]` above `fn map(owns f: F)`). `[FN-6]` makes it worse: "Callable types are compared by their parameter types and words, their result, `unsafe` and `thread_shared`" omits `once`, so `once fn() -> int` and `fn() -> int` compare equal there and differ in `[CLO-6]`; a compiler must choose. The grammar parses the fix (`fn_type := ["once"] ["unsafe"] ... "fn"`, with `thread_shared` before a `base_type`).
verdicts.better_fix: As proposed. In `[FN-6]` write the coercion in `[CLO-6]`'s own words: "a function that gives no capture away meets both `fn(…)` and `once fn(…)` of its shape; one that does meets only `once fn(…)`, and given where `fn(…)` is wanted is `E3013` (`[CLO-6]`)". The `std` signatures and the `E3013` registry row ("a plain `once fn()` parameter") are unchanged in meaning.

verdicts.reason: Three of the four points are real. `max`/`min`: `[THR-21]` lists "`max`, `min`" among the forms of "A task's `total += e` (and `-=`, ...)" with no written statement, while the same rule says "a task that reads the current value (`if stats.total < 10: stats.total += x`) need[s] a lock (`E7007`)" and `best = max(best, part.len())` reads `best`; `[PAR-3]` gives a form only for `@parallel(reduce=[... best: max])`. `m[k] op= e`: "Each task's accumulator has the place's type" names an `int` for `counts[part]`, which cannot hold two tasks' different keys, and whether a task's key absent from `counts` is inserted at the join is unsaid. `static mut`: `[THR-20]` says "two tasks changing it ... is `E7007`, other than by a reduction, under a lock or through an `Atomic`" while `[THR-21]` admits a reduction only "on a local, or on a field of an object the tasks reach"; `SEEN += 1` is neither. The `thread_shared` field is answered: `[THR-1]` says "**no owner changes a `thread_shared` value directly** (`E7014` ...); its state changes only through an `Atomic`, a `Mutex`, an `RwLock`, a channel end, or a field `guarded by` a lock", and a reduction's combining write at the join is none of these, so `st.total += x` on a `thread_shared st` is `E7014` with no further word. Verdict 105 is untouched by the proposal.
verdicts.narrowed_to: The written form of the `max`/`min` reduction, the accumulator and join of `P[k] op= e` with per-task keys, and whether a `static mut` is a reduction place are unsaid; a `thread_shared` field is already `E7014` by `[THR-1]`.
verdicts.better_fix: As proposed, with the `thread_shared` sentence reduced to a cross-reference: "A field of a `thread_shared` value is not a reduction place: its owners never change it directly (`E7014`, `[THR-1]`), and the message gives the `Atomic` or the `guarded by` field."

verdicts.reason: The guard in a plain local is a real gap: `[THR-19]` conditions every refusal on "Inside a lock's `with` block", `[THR-3]` allows a guard elsewhere ("the mutex is released when the guard ends, which `with g = m.lock():` places at the end of the block"), and `[THR-6]` makes `MutexGuard` not `@must_drop` ("The standard library applies it to `Scope` and `JobScope` only"), so `g = m.lock()` followed by `HANDLER()` is a wait for a held lock the text never refuses. The static's first access is real too: `[STA-3]` runs the initialiser "on first access", which is not a call, and `[EFF-24]` computes "which locks it may take" "from the functions it calls". The second `read()` is real: `[THR-19]` names "its `write()` while this thread holds its `read()`, or the reverse" and `[THR-3]` states no policy for a writer waiting between two readers, so whether the program waits for ever depends on the runtime, against `[THR-19]`'s title "refused when compiling". The foreign call is already covered: `[THR-19]` refuses "a direct call that may take the held lock and is not proved to enter past it", and `[EFF-26]` makes "a call of a foreign function count[] as possibly running every callback C keeps, on the threads their contracts allow, and makes the changes they make, for its caller and every function that calls it, unless the foreign function's declaration says `@ffi(no_callbacks)`", over "the same call graph" from which `[EFF-24]` works out "which locks it may take"; naming it in `[THR-19]` is harmless but adds no rule.
verdicts.narrowed_to: `[THR-19]` must hold while a guard in a plain local is in use, must count a `static`'s first-access initialiser as a direct call of it, and must say what a second `read()` under a held `read()` does; the foreign call is covered by `[THR-19]`'s direct-call clause with `[EFF-26]`.
verdicts.better_fix: As proposed for the opening sentence and the `static` and `read()` items; the foreign-call item may be kept as an example of the direct-call clause ("a foreign call not declared `@ffi(no_callbacks)` is such a direct call, by the callbacks C keeps, `[EFF-26]`"). The `E7018` registry row ("inside that lock's `with` block") changes with it to "while this thread holds that lock".

verdicts.reason: `[THR-18]` gives the block no name for what it holds: "A `Lock` is a lock with no value inside; `with x.lock:` holds it for the block", and its only identity condition is on the object ("on the same object `x` (the same name, not given another object in the block ...)"), which `log.lock = Lock()` does not break: it gives the field, not `log`, another value. For a `Mutex` the text is safe without a new rule, since `[THR-3]` makes the guard "a view of `m` that reads through to `ref mut T`" and `[BRW-1]` keeps a `ref mut` name alone (`E3022` for `m = Mutex(1)` while `g` is used); the `Lock` form alone has no view. No rule says a `Lock` field is set once (`[CLS-9]` speaks of `let` fields only; Annex A's "never replaced; changed by its own operations" is a comment on a `static`, not a rule). The reader's first sentence is the right and general fix; its second sentence (every lock, atomic and `Once` field `let`-like, `E3023`) is not needed and refuses harmless programs: a replacement while no guard is in use breaks nothing, a replacement under a scoped task is already `E7007` (`[THR-11]`: the task changes the lock by its own operation while the parent changes it), and one of a `thread_shared` value's field is already `E7014`.
verdicts.better_fix: Add to `[THR-18]`, after "`with x.lock:` holds it for the block.": "The block holds a read-only view of `x.lock` whose life is the block, as `with g = m.lock():` holds `g` (`[THR-3]`, `[BRW-1]`, `[BRW-2]`): while it runs, `x.lock` is not given another value, swapped or taken out, and `x` is not handed over, ended or given another value, through any name (`E3021` for the change of what the view reads, `E3060` where the change reshapes or ends what it points into: \"`log.lock = Lock()` (line 10) replaces the lock this block holds (line 9), whose end would release a lock never taken; give the log a new lock after the block, or keep the one made with it\")." Nothing else changes; `[THR-19]`'s and `[BRW-20]`'s rules apply to the view as to a guard.

verdicts.reason: `[BLD-14]` item 6 reads "the locks a function may take; and"; `[EFF-24]` records "which locks it may take, or needs held (`[THR-18]`)"; `[THR-18]` makes the second fact decide a call across the edge: "A function whose body uses a guarded field without taking its lock is worked out to need that lock held (its summary, `[EFF-24]`), and is called only where the lock is held (`E7013`)". `[EFF-4]` records "each function's effect set and summary (`[EFF-24]`)" whole, so the fact is recorded; `[BLD-14]`'s enumeration is the one place that leaves it out, which `[BLD-2]`'s interface hashes and `[DIA-22]` read. Text only, as the reader says.

`[PRF-1]`: "Every profile ... stops in the same places with the same messages, and computes the same results. The one check that differs is `debug_assert`"; `[PRF-4]`: "The checks that run while a program runs are the same in every profile". `[PRF-3]`'s table allows "C sanitizers (`sanitizers = […]`) | allowed | allowed | not allowed", and a sanitizer stops a `development` build where `release` runs on. No sentence of Part XVII places the sanitizer outside the guarantee; the proposed sentence does, in one line, without changing any check. Minor.

`[CLI-21]`: "foreign calls and threads are unavailable (`E6010`); results equal a compiled run's"; `[CT-2]`'s `E6010` names "a thread". A `@parallel` loop runs "on the job system (§XI.5)", a pool of worker threads, yet `[PAR-4]` lets "the calling thread run[] the chunk itself" and `[PAR-5]` promises the same bits "whatever the worker count", so a one-thread run is within what a compiled program may do; `[CT-4]` even requires that "the test suite runs every program both compiled and on the evaluator". So an evaluator may refuse or run the loop and both readings satisfy the sentences: a guess. The proposal's "a job scope run on the one thread" is not safe in the same way: two jobs of one `jobs.scope()` may wait on each other through a channel, which a compiled run serves with two workers and a one-thread run never does, and `[PAR-4]`'s own-thread fallback is stated for `@parallel` only.
verdicts.better_fix: In `[CLI-21]`, replace "foreign calls and threads are unavailable (`E6010`)" with "foreign calls, `thread.spawn`, `thread.scope`, `jobs.submit` and `jobs.scope` are unavailable (`E6010`); a `@parallel` loop runs on the one thread, chunk by chunk in chunk order, as `[PAR-4]`'s calling thread may in any run, and gives the same bits (`[PAR-5]`)".

verdicts.reason: `[DIA-6a]`: "Each code is defined by exactly one rule." The registry's header says each row gives "what it reports and the rule it enforces", and rows name several: `E7015` → `[THR-1]`, `[THR-2]`, `[THR-10]`, `[CLO-16]`, `[FFI-22]`; `E3020` → `[BRW-18]`, `[CTL-2]`; `E9001` → `[MAN-1]`, `[PRF-3]`; `E3013` → `[OWN-11]`, `[EXP-6]`, `[CLO-6]`. `[TST-4b]` ("a rule that names a code needs one per code") is consistent with either reading, but `tools/rule_index.py` under `[TST-4]`/`[DIA-6]` has no rule for which row owns the page. The proposed text resolves it without changing any case. Text only.

missed: [THR-11] "under a lock" does not say which lock: a place no lock guards, changed by two tasks each inside a `with` block of some lock, is literally "under a lock". Program: `class Stats:` with `lock: Lock = Lock()` and `total: int = 0` (not `guarded by`); two tasks `scope.spawn(owns fn(): with stats.lock: stats.total += 1)` and `scope.spawn(owns fn(): with other.lock: stats.total += 1)` — the second holds another object's lock, and even the first is a plain field changed inside a `with` of a lock that does not guard it. A compiler must guess whether "under a lock" means any `with` block or the lock that guards the place (`[THR-18]`'s `guarded by`, a `Mutex`/`RwLock`'s content through its guard, `[THR-3]`). The better text for `[THR-11]` given under G5-01 ("through the lock that guards the place") closes it; the `E7007` registry row's "under a lock" changes the same way.

[BLD-FFI-3] names the manifest key `link = ["vulkan-1"]` while §XVII.2 and `[MAN-8]` name `[link]` with `libs = ["m"]`, and `[MAN-1]` makes an unknown key `E9001`. Program: an `ember.toml` with `[link]` and `link = ["vulkan-1"]` as `[BLD-FFI-3]` writes it, which `[MAN-8]`'s list refuses, or `libs = ["vulkan-1"]`, which `[BLD-FFI-3]` does not describe. Text only: replace `[BLD-FFI-3]`'s "(`link = ["vulkan-1"]`)" with "(`[link] libs = ["vulkan-1"]`, `[MAN-8]`)".

[THR-20] says a `static mut` "is reached only by the main thread and the tasks of scopes it opens" and lists among the other-thread functions "a job submitted outside a scope"; a job of a `jobs.scope()` block, which `[JOB-2]` makes follow `[THR-5]` and `[THR-11]` and which runs on a worker thread, is in neither list. Program: `static mut FRAME: int = 0` and, in `main`, `with s = jobs.scope(): s.submit(owns fn(): FRAME += 1)` — `E7012` or a reduction checked by `[THR-11]`? A compiler must guess. Proposed: in `[THR-20]`, write "by the main thread and the tasks and jobs of the scopes it opens (`[THR-11]`, `[JOB-2]`)" in place of "by the main thread and the tasks of scopes it opens", and the same in `[THR-13]`'s module-variable bullet and `[STA-1]`'s "the main thread and its scoped tasks".
